sections.heading: Giving you the praise you deserve
sections.text:
God, it is right for me to praise you. This is not a small thing or a religious extra; it is one of the best and truest things I can do.

Everything you have made shows something of who you are and carries out your purposes. The sea and the land, the cold of winter and the heat of summer, the light of morning and the quiet of evening all speak of you. You fill my ordinary world with your gifts, and you give them generously for me to receive with gratitude.
theological_themes: God is worthy of praise from all creation.
Creation reveals God’s attributes and purposes.
Ordinary created gifts are to be received with gratitude and enjoyment before God.

scripture_references.connection: This psalm opens with the fittingness of praise being offered to God, which directly supports the prayer’s sense that worship is God’s due and the worshiper’s highest work.
The heavens are described as declaring God’s glory, grounding the prayer’s claim that creation displays who God is rather than existing as a spiritually empty backdrop.
Paul says God richly provides everything to enjoy, which supports receiving the natural world and daily gifts with thankful delight rather than suspicion or entitlement.

sections.heading: Remembering that you rule over everything
sections.text:
You are King over every king and Lord over every lord. Nations, rulers, and empires do not stand because they are ultimate; they rise and fall under your hand and according to your will.

All you have made praises you, and your people bless your name. Please count me among those who belong to you. Make me more like your holy people in heart and life, and give me the humble place of a disciple, sitting at Jesus’ feet and learning from him.
theological_themes: God is sovereign over rulers, nations, and history.
God’s people respond to his reign with blessing and worship.
The believer desires to belong among God’s holy people and to learn from Christ.

scripture_references.connection: The title “King of kings and Lord of lords” names Christ’s supreme authority over every earthly power, matching the prayer’s confession that no empire or ruler is ultimate.

This passage joins the praise of all God’s works with the blessing of his saints and celebrates his everlasting kingdom, closely reflecting this section’s movement from creation’s praise to God’s people worshiping his reign.
Mary’s posture at Jesus’ feet represents attentive discipleship, illuminating the prayer’s desire not merely to be counted among the holy but to be teachable before Christ.

sections.heading: Asking you to shape my whole inner life by your Word
sections.text:
Let my faith be deeply rooted in your Word, not in my moods, opinions, or passing ideas. Teach my mind by your truth. Set my desires on what is holy and lasting. Make my motives plain and clean before you.

Do not let my heart be twisted away from you, even when I can still look religious on the outside. Keep me honest with you all the way down.
theological_themes: True religion must be grounded in Scripture.
God must renew the mind, affections, motives, and heart.
External religion is not enough if the heart is wrong before God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers to let Christ’s word dwell richly in them, grounding the prayer’s request for faith to be rooted in God’s Word rather than self-made spirituality.
The renewing of the mind by God’s transforming work supports the request for understanding shaped by divine truth rather than the patterns of the age.
David’s plea for a clean heart and renewed spirit gives biblical language to the prayer’s concern that motives and inner life be made right before God.

sections.heading: Asking for protection from what is in me and around me
sections.text:
Rescue me from the darkness that still clouds my mind, from the corruption still living in my heart, and from the temptations I meet every day. I am not as strong as I like to think I am. I am in danger as long as I live in this fallen world.

Keep your watchful eye on me. Defend me from the enemies of my soul—whether they come through the world, the devil, or my own sinful desires. Save me also from the painful consequences I have brought on myself by my own foolishness and sin. Have mercy on me, and guard me.
theological_themes: The believer remains dependent on God because of indwelling sin, spiritual danger, and temptation.
God is asked to protect his people from evil and from the enemies of the soul.
Some suffering is connected to human sin and foolishness, and mercy is needed even there.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches his disciples to ask the Father not to lead them into temptation but to deliver them from evil, directly grounding this section’s plea for protection.
Peter warns believers of a real spiritual adversary while also pointing them to God’s restoring and strengthening grace, matching the prayer’s sober sense of danger and dependence.
James explains that temptation is also drawn out from within by disordered desire, supporting the prayer’s honesty about danger coming not only from outside enemies but from the believer’s own heart.

sections.heading: Living with Jesus until the day I finally see him
sections.text:
Until the full day of life breaks in your presence, keep me in open, unhindered fellowship with Jesus. Until I receive the inheritance you have promised in full, let me taste now the pledge of it through your Spirit.

And until I finish the path you have given me, help me run it with joy and steady effort. Let my life show what you have given your people in Christ. In everything, make the truth about you beautiful through the way I live.
theological_themes: The Christian life is lived in fellowship with Christ while awaiting final glory.
The Holy Spirit is the pledge and first taste of the believer’s inheritance.
Believers are called to finish their course with joy and to live in a way that commends the doctrine of God.

scripture_references.connection: John describes Christian fellowship as fellowship with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ, supporting the prayer’s desire for real communion with Jesus now.
Paul calls the Holy Spirit the guarantee of the believer’s inheritance, which directly explains the prayer’s language of tasting now what will one day be fully received.
Paul speaks of finishing his course and ministry with joy, grounding the prayer’s request to complete the God-given path with perseverance and gladness.
Paul says believers can adorn the doctrine of God by their conduct, which supports the closing desire that daily life make God’s truth visible and beautiful.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s request to be saved from “all painful evils” could be misunderstood as asking for a suffering-free life. I rendered it as a plea for mercy and protection, especially from self-caused consequences, without implying that faithful Christians are promised exemption from suffering.

The prayer’s language about the “natural darkness” of the mind and “corruptions” of the heart reflects a strong Puritan doctrine of remaining sin and human inability apart from grace. I preserved that unsparing self-assessment rather than softening it into general weakness.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Resemble them in character and condition” was interpreted as a desire to share both the holiness and the belonging of God’s people, not as a request for identical earthly circumstances.
“Sit with them at Jesus’ feet” was rendered as humble discipleship and teachability before Christ, drawing on the biblical image of Mary listening to Jesus.

“Until the day of life dawns above” and “until fruition comes” were interpreted eschatologically: the believer waits for full life in God’s presence and the completed inheritance, while enjoying the Spirit’s present pledge.
“Display the resources of the Christian” was rendered as showing in daily life what God gives his people in Christ, rather than as self-generated moral strength.
